title: Alberta has tabled a bill for new riding maps. What could a court challenge mean?
summary: Alberta’s controversial new riding map is one step closer to implementation after Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled a bill in the legislature on Monday. But legal experts say a potential court…

image.caption: Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled Bill 40, the proposed Electoral Divisions Act, in the legislature on Monday. It would repeal the current Electoral Divisions Act, adopting the new ridings as proposed by an independent advisory panel. (CBC News)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Alberta’s controversial new riding map is one step closer to implementation after Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled a bill in the legislature on Monday. But legal experts say a potential court challenge could introduce a high level of uncertainty in advance of the next provincial election.
Legal experts say possible challenge could introduce high level of uncertainty
Alberta’s controversial new riding map is one step closer to implementation after Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled a bill in the legislature on Monday.
But legal experts say a potential court challenge could introduce a high level of uncertainty in advance of the next provincial election, set for Oct. 18, 2027.
Earlier this month, an advisory panel issued a report on Alberta’s electoral boundaries following a government-led process that saw an initial commission’s riding plan discarded.
Among other changes, it proposes expanding a few Calgary ridings across municipal boundaries and establishing a sole urban seat for Lethbridge, along with three hybrid urban-rural seats.

blocks.text: For three decades, updates to these maps, delivered by bipartisan commissions, have been enacted without much fanfare or controversy.

But this go-around has been marked by accusations of U.S.-style “gerrymandering” — a process in which politicians redraw voting lines so as to provide a boost to their own electoral chances — and threats of a possible court challenge from the Opposition NDP on constitutional grounds.
Alberta NDP accuses Smith of ‘Trump-style’ gerrymandering in new electoral map
The governing UCP previously signed off on the new political boundaries. The bill will now be debated in the House, and Amery has said he expects the legislation to pass by the end of the year.
On the possibility of an injunction

Stephen Thiele, a partner at Gardiner Roberts in Toronto, said a court challenge would involve an application to challenge the constitutionality of the bill, likely under Section 3 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which is concerned with voters’ rights.
Parties could ask for an injunction to prevent the bill from taking effect, and to hold the election based on the current ridings that are in place, he said.
“I would assume that government lawyers would argue that this is not the appropriate time for an injunction,” Thiele said.
"The legislation has taken effect. Elections Alberta has already done its work, and spent a lot of money. They would raise that argument."

Such a Charter challenge would zero in on the right to “effective representation,” the legal principle that allows for the balancing of equal-sized voter populations with other factors, like geography.
Thiele said it's not clear whether any challenge — from the NDP or another group — would be successful.

In part citing delays a legal challenge would pose, Elections Alberta chief electoral officer Gordon McClure wrote in a letter in late October that the government should maintain the electoral boundaries currently in place or postpone the next election.

It’s possible that the elections agency may have to prepare for two different scenarios — one in which the new boundaries come into effect and one in which the old ones are in effect, according to Marion Sandilands, a constitutional lawyer and partner at Conway Litigation.
“Whenever Section 3 challenges happen close to an election, it creates a lot of uncertainty about how the election is to be administered,” Sandilands said.

“Any court hearing this kind of challenge, and if it had an injunction request in it, the court would have to take into account how the election can be administered properly … the closer we get to the election, the higher risk it becomes for the running of the election.”

Amery denied McClure’s request to maintain the prior boundaries or postpone the next election, writing in a letter that the province saw “no value” in considering hypothetical judicial outcomes at this time.
“The final electoral boundaries enacted by the Legislative Assembly will constitute the law of Alberta, and Elections Alberta is expected to prepare accordingly,” he wrote.
He went on to say that other Canadian jurisdictions have demonstrated that electoral administrators could implement revised boundaries and administer elections within "substantially shorter periods.”

blocks.text: Challenge to come after royal assent: Nenshi
Naheed Nenshi, the leader of the Opposition, reiterated the NDP's “gerrymandering” characterizations on Monday.
“There is still time for the UCP to do the right thing. They can vote against adopting these gerrymandered maps,” Nenshi told reporters.
While he would not detail next steps, Nenshi said “every lawyer knows” that a bill can only be challenged once it has received royal assent.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, meanwhile, has said her government will assemble a legal team to make the case that the new proposed electoral boundaries achieve effective representation.
Brian O’Ferrall, a retired Alberta Court of Appeal justice who led the advisory panel, wrote in an executive summary that he believes the proposals suggested in the report are "not unconstitutional."
